The best chain is QB7-QB12-QB11, with QB12 in the middle. I read the current default calibration of the real Garnet chip (set 9069c4ef-7ab6-4e50-be4f-c91d71c3a06d). Then I checked every chain of 3 connected qubits. The QB12-QB11 pair has an IRB CZ fidelity of 0.99945. The QB12-QB7 pair has 0.99907. Their product is 0.99852, the highest of any chain. The next best chain is QB11-QB12-QB17, at 0.99818.

I built a 3-qubit GHZ circuit on exactly those qubits. It puts QB12 into an equal mix of 0 and 1. Then two CZ gates, one on QB12-QB7 and one on QB12-QB11, copy that state onto the two outer qubits. Single-qubit rotations sit around each CZ. At the end it measures all 3 qubits. I read the circuit back from the server. It has 2 CZ gates, on [QB12, QB7] and [QB12, QB11], and it measures QB7, QB12, and QB11.

I ran it on garnet:mock with 200 shots (job 01a16482-6ea0-70f0-bb08-64a59e097d90). The bit order is QB7, QB12, QB11. The counts were 000: 48, 001: 47, 110: 61, 111: 44. The mock cost 0 credits.

These counts do not show entanglement. The mock checks that the circuit is valid on Garnet and then returns random results. It does not simulate the circuit. I simulated the submitted circuit without noise. It gives 000 half the time and 111 half the time, and nothing else. That is the GHZ principle: the 3 qubits are linked, so a measurement finds them all 0 or all 1, never mixed. On the real Garnet chip you would see mostly 000 and 111. A few other results would show up from gate and readout errors. Picking the chain with the best CZ fidelities is meant to keep those errors low.
